title: Arcade play sessions with a 30-minute timeout
prompt:
An online arcade logs a row for every action a player takes. Analysts want play sessions: a player's session ends when more than 30 minutes pass before their next action. A gap of exactly 30 minutes stays in the same session.

Return one row per session.

- Columns: player_id, session_start, session_end, events, minutes
- session_start and session_end are the first and last action times as text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI'
- events counts the action rows in the session (duplicates at the same instant each count)
- minutes is the whole minutes from first to last action (0 for a single action)
- Order by player_id, then session_start
- Sessions can cross midnight
hints: Look at the time since the same player's previous action. Which window function gives you that?
Mark a row 1 when it starts a new session (no previous action, or gap > 30 minutes), else 0. A running sum of those marks numbers the sessions.

CASE WHEN event_at - lag(event_at) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_at) <= interval '30 minutes' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, then sum(...) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_at) with the default RANGE frame so rows at the same instant get the same session. Group and format with to_char.

exercise.starter:
-- Sessions per player (bucketed by clock hour for now)
SELECT player_id,
       to_char(min(event_at), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS session_start,
       to_char(max(event_at), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS session_end,
       count(*) AS events,
       (extract(epoch FROM max(event_at) - min(event_at)) / 60)::int AS minutes
FROM arcade_events
GROUP BY player_id, date_trunc('hour', event_at)
ORDER BY player_id, min(event_at);
exercise.solution:
WITH e AS (
  SELECT player_id, event_at,
         CASE WHEN event_at - lag(event_at) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_at)
                   <= interval '30 minutes'
              THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new
  FROM arcade_events
), s AS (
  SELECT player_id, event_at,
         sum(is_new) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_at) AS session_no
  FROM e
)
SELECT player_id,
       to_char(min(event_at), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS session_start,
       to_char(max(event_at), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS session_end,
       count(*) AS events,
       (extract(epoch FROM max(event_at) - min(event_at)) / 60)::int AS minutes
FROM s
GROUP BY player_id, session_no
ORDER BY player_id, min(event_at);

tests.name: long session and a single action
exactly 30 minutes stays in the session

hiddenTests.name: 31 minute gap splits and inserts out of order

explanation: Sessionization is gaps and islands on time: lag() measures the gap to the same player's previous action, a CASE turns 'no previous action or gap over 30 minutes' into a 1, and a running sum of those flags gives every row its session number. The comparison is <= interval '30 minutes', so an exact 30-minute gap stays inside; a NULL lag makes the comparison NULL and falls to ELSE 1. A subtle trap is duplicate timestamps: with a ROWS frame the two tied rows could get different running sums depending on peer order, while the default RANGE frame gives peers the same sum. Bucketing by clock hour or by date is the usual wrong answer; it splits sessions that cross the hour or midnight and merges unrelated actions.
notes: An index on (player_id, event_at) lets both windows run without a sort. On big event tables, sessionization is often done incrementally: store each player's last event time and current session id, and only process new events. Timestamps here are timestamp without time zone; with timestamptz, to_char uses the session TimeZone, so set it explicitly when formatting.
followUps: Return the average session length per player, excluding single-action sessions.
